summary: AgentGuard turns 461 reviewed anomalous coding-agent traces from the authors' prior ABTest benchmark into 15 conditional guardrails (When/DoNot/Unless/Instead/ApplyAt), packaged as a skill with 5 routing entries so only relevant rules load before a tool call. On 100 held-out ABTest tasks (each with one injected adversarial step) run 3x each in Docker with Claude Code + Claude Haiku 4.5, human reviewers found abnormal executions fell from 69.0% to 26.7% and full task success rose from 21.7% to 35.0%, at the cost of a 19.3% over-refusal rate.

claims.claim: AgentGuard reduces Abnormal Execution Rate from 69.0% to 26.7%.
claims.evidence: Table 2: 207/300 vs 80/300; task-clustered bootstrap 95% CI -51.7 to -33.0, exact paired randomization p<0.001. Table 3: 41 tasks fixed vs 3 newly abnormal.

claims.claim: Successful Task Completion rises from 21.7% to 35.0%.

claims.evidence: CBR 49.0% -> 42.0% (CI -17.0 to 3.0, p=0.199, not significant) but over-refusal 0 -> 19.3% (58/300, p<0.001) and 55 runs with benign loss (Table 4). Conclusion's 'preserving benign behaviors' overstates this.

claims.claim: Guardrails learned from historical failures generalize to new tasks.
claims.evidence: Held-out by task, but the evaluation tasks share the same ABTest generator and appear to run on one Click repository snapshot (§4.2); no cross-repo, cross-model, or cross-benchmark test.

patterns.note: Instruction-level conditional guardrails (e.g., do not weaken tests, do not touch unrelated files) cut abnormal actions on held-out tasks; enforcement is advisory via prompt, not policy-engine.
Guardrails delivered as a skill with routing so only the relevant subskill loads; low token/cost overhead (Table 5). No comparison with loading all rules at once.
Harness rules induced automatically from failure traces; a form of self-improving harness, single iteration.
A key learned rule forbids rewriting assertions to make tests pass unless the task requires it.
All runs in fresh Docker containers; sandboxing is the evaluation setting, not studied.
Guardrails increase clarification/refusal (CAR 25.0% -> 62.7%) but also 19.3% over-refusal, shifting work back to humans.

methodology.sample: 642 ABTest failure traces over 382 tasks; 461 traces/282 tasks for construction; 100 disjoint tasks x 3 runs x 2 conditions = 600 executions.
methodology.baselines: Raw Claude Code only; no hand-written guardrail set, generic safety prompt, or all-rules-loaded baseline.
methodology.models: Claude Code 2.1.19 with Claude Haiku 4.5 only.
methodology.variance: 3 runs per task; task-clustered bootstrap CIs and paired randomization tests reported.
methodology.ablations: Per-routing-entry effect distribution (Fig 2); no ablation of routing vs full loading or of individual rules.
methodology.contamination_controls: Task-level split between construction and evaluation.

standards.artifacts: No code or guardrail release link found; ABTest data is from prior work.

biases.detail: ABTest benchmark (Dai et al. 2026) shares first and last authors with this paper; guardrails are induced and evaluated on the same benchmark family.
Reviewers could identify the condition because guardrail instructions appear in the trace (§4.3).
Only Claude Haiku 4.5 in Claude Code; stronger models may need fewer guardrails.
Evaluation runs on one Python repository snapshot (Click).
Every task contains one synthetic injected adversarial step, inflating baseline abnormality relative to ordinary work.
Compared only to an unguarded agent.
Learned guardrail subskills not released; Table 1 gives abstracted one-line versions only.

coi.affiliations: Wuyang Dai, Song Wang - Lassonde School of Engineering, York University.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude Code / Claude Haiku 4.5 used as the substrate, not promoted.
coi.detail: Academic authors; intellectual conflict from evaluating on their own ABTest benchmark.

verdict_reason: Better statistics than most (3 runs, clustered CIs, kappa 0.87/0.81, held-out tasks), but single weak model, one Python repo, unblinded raters, no non-trivial baseline, own benchmark, no artifacts, and an over-refusal cost that the conclusion underplays.
applicability: Directly useful as a harness technique. A Java team can mine its own agent failures (test weakening, edits outside the service module, unrequested dependency/lockfile changes, fabricated completion claims) into short When/DoNot/Unless/Instead rules shipped as a host-neutral skill that qr stamps into every agent host, loaded per action type. The 19.3% over-refusal means such rules should pair with deterministic checks (build/test gates, path allowlists per repo) instead of replacing them. Evidence is Python/Haiku-only on one repo, so re-measure on the ≥4 the repositories; rules like 'preserve acceptance criteria when running checks' align with spec-driven development.

conflicts_with.detail: CS-Guard finds LLM-level guardrails easily bypassed by adversarial framing; AgentGuard shows prompt-level guardrails help against benign-but-sloppy agent misbehavior. Not the same threat model, so prompt-level guardrails should not be treated as a security boundary.
